title: Rotate Image
pattern: matrix index mapping / rotating a grid in one pass
statement:
You are given a rectangular matrix of integers with `R` rows and `C` columns, where every row has the same length. Rotate it 90 degrees clockwise and return the rotated matrix.

Under a clockwise rotation the element at row `i`, column `j` moves to row `j`, column `R - 1 - i` of the result, so the result has `C` rows and `R` columns. The input matrix must not be modified.

Constraints: `1 <= matrix.length <= 30`, `1 <= matrix[0].length <= 30` and `-100 <= matrix[i][j] <= 100`.

constraints: Inputs are JSON-serializable values satisfying the bounds stated above.
hints: Pick one corner cell and write down exactly where it lands after the rotation. Do that for two cells and the pattern appears.
The output has as many rows as the input has columns, so the two dimensions swap in the result.
Do not search for the source of each output cell. Walk the input instead and place every element with `out[j][rows - 1 - i] = matrix[i][j]`.

editorial.approach: The brute force treats the destination as unknown and searches for it: for every output cell `(r, c)` it walks all source cells `(i, j)` looking for the single pair with `i = R - 1 - c` and `j = r`, and copies that value. Every output cell costs a full matrix scan, so the work is O((R·C)²) with the same asymptotic memory as the answer. The optimal derives the mapping once and inverts it: instead of asking where each output cell comes from, it asks where each source cell goes, and writes `out[j][R - 1 - i] = matrix[i][j]` in a single double loop over the input, which is one read and one write per element.
editorial.why_optimal: The result contains R·C values and every one of them must be written, so Ω(R·C) is a hard lower bound for any algorithm that returns the rotated matrix, and the direct index mapping reaches it. The brute force multiplies that by the number of cells again because it discovers the mapping by exhaustive search instead of computing it. At the capped size of 30×30 the brute force is about 8·10^5 inner steps, fast enough to be a valid checkpoint, but the one-pass version stays linear no matter how the bounds grow.
editorial.pitfalls: Writing `out[j][i]`, which is a transpose and not a rotation, and happens to be correct-looking on symmetric test data. Using `C - 1 - i` instead of `R - 1 - i`: the constant comes from the number of rows, so the bug only shows up on non-square matrices. Allocating the result with the source dimensions (`R` rows instead of `C`), which throws or silently drops the last row. Rotating counter-clockwise by swapping the two reversed axes. And mutating the input in place when the statement asks for a returned copy.
